title: The Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex: The One-Way Gate to the Cycle

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) turns pyruvate, the three-carbon end of glycolysis, into {{c1::acetyl-CoA}}, releasing a carbon as CO₂ and banking one NADH.
cards.quote: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) turns pyruvate, the three-carbon end of glycolysis, into acetyl-CoA, releasing a carbon as CO₂ and banking one NADH.

cards.front: Write the net reaction of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
cards.back: Pyruvate + CoA + NAD⁺ → Acetyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH + H⁺
cards.quote: The net reaction is worth memorizing exactly: Pyruvate + CoA + NAD⁺ → Acetyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH + H⁺

cards.front: Why is the PDC reaction called an oxidative decarboxylation?
cards.back: Pyruvate (3 carbons) loses its carboxyl carbon as CO₂ (decarboxylation), and the remaining two carbons are oxidized to an acetyl group carried by CoA (oxidation). The two halves happen at different moments.
cards.quote: It is an oxidative decarboxylation: pyruvate (3 carbons) loses its carboxyl carbon as CO₂ and is oxidized to a 2-carbon acetyl group carried by coenzyme A.

cards.front: In which compartment does PDC run, and how does pyruvate from glycolysis get there?
cards.back: The mitochondrial matrix. Pyruvate crosses the inner membrane on the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier.
cards.quote: It runs in the mitochondrial matrix, which pyruvate enters through the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier.

cards.front: In PDC, the two acetyl carbons and the two electrons removed from them ride the same lipoamide arm. Where does each get off?
cards.back: The carbons get off at E2, onto CoA. The electrons get off at E3, through FAD to NAD⁺.
cards.why: The carboxyl carbon has already left as CO₂ at E1, before any oxidation happens.
cards.quote: they get off at different stops: the carbons at E2 (onto CoA), the electrons at E3 (through FAD to NAD⁺).

cards.front: Rank a carbon's oxidation level from least to most oxidized: acid, alcohol, aldehyde.
cards.back: Alcohol, then aldehyde, then acid, each with one more bond to oxygen in place of a bond to hydrogen.
cards.quote: Chemists rank a carbon's oxidation level by those bonds: alcohol, then aldehyde, then acid, each with one more.
cards.section: Following one pyruvate: two tracks on one arm

cards.front: What lets thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) on E1 attack pyruvate and release CO₂?
cards.back: Its ring carbon between a nitrogen and a sulfur can drop its hydrogen, become negatively charged and grab pyruvate's middle carbon. The ring then soaks up electrons, so the carboxyl group breaks away as CO₂.
cards.quote: It can drop its hydrogen, become negatively charged and grab pyruvate's middle carbon.
cards.section: Following one pyruvate: two tracks on one arm

cards.front: How can PDC's lipoamide arm carry an acetyl group and two electrons at the same time?
cards.back: Its S–S bond breaks into two –SH groups when it takes two electrons (with two protons). One sulfur holds the acetyl group as a thioester; the broken S–S holds the electrons.
cards.quote: So the arm can carry two things at once: an acetyl group on one sulfur, and two electrons in the broken S–S.
cards.section: Following one pyruvate: two tracks on one arm

cards.front: Name the three enzymes of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
cards.back: E1, pyruvate dehydrogenase; E2, dihydrolipoyl transacetylase; E3, dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase.
cards.quote: Step 3 · Acetyl transfer · E2 (dihydrolipoyl transacetylase)

cards.front: In PDC step 1 on E1, pyruvate's carboxyl carbon leaves as CO₂. Are any electrons removed from the substrate at this step?
cards.back: No. CO₂ leaves its bonding pair behind on TPP's ring, so the two carbons left on TPP sit at the oxidation level of an aldehyde. The oxidation comes in step 2.
cards.quote: CO₂ leaves its bonding electron pair behind (TPP's ring soaks it up), so no electrons leave the molecule overall
cards.section: Following one pyruvate: two tracks on one arm

cards.front: Yeast pyruvate decarboxylase uses the same TPP chemistry as PDC's E1. Predict its two-carbon product and whether NADH forms.
cards.back: It releases acetaldehyde, and no NADH forms. Without the oxidative transfer step, the two carbons stay at aldehyde level, and no NAD⁺ is involved.
cards.why: TPP decarboxylation removes no electrons; only the later oxidation onto lipoamide does.
cards.quote: Yeast's pyruvate decarboxylase uses the same TPP chemistry but releases acetaldehyde for fermentation, with no NAD⁺ involved.
cards.section: Following one pyruvate: two tracks on one arm

cards.front: Which PDC enzyme makes the complex's only NADH, and from what?
cards.back: E3 (dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase), in step 4, passing electrons from its bound FADH₂ to NAD⁺.
cards.quote: This is the only NADH-producing step of the whole complex.

cards.front: In PDC the oxidation happens at E1, in step 2. Why is NADH not made there?
cards.back: E1 has no NAD⁺ site. The electrons go onto the nearest acceptor, the arm's disulfide, and ride the arm to E3, the only enzyme that can hand them to NAD⁺.
cards.quote: That is the exam trap in one line: the oxidation is at E1, but the NADH is made at E3.
cards.section: Following one pyruvate: two tracks on one arm

cards.front: FADH₂ forms during the PDC mechanism. Why does the net reaction list NADH and not FADH₂?
cards.back: The FADH₂ is a moment-long internal relay on E3. It never leaves the enzyme; its electrons pass on to NAD⁺.
cards.quote: The FADH₂ along the way never leaves E3, which is why the net reaction lists NADH, not FADH₂.
cards.section: Following one pyruvate: two tracks on one arm

cards.front: PDC step 4 at E3 makes no carbon product. Why must it happen before the complex can run again?
cards.back: It restores the lipoamide disulfide. An arm still holding two electrons as –SH groups cannot accept the next acetyl group.
cards.quote: Step 4 makes no product carbon, but it has to happen: an arm still holding electrons cannot accept the next acetyl group.
cards.section: Following one pyruvate: two tracks on one arm

cards.front: List PDC's five coenzymes in the order pyruvate meets them.
cards.back: TPP (step 1), lipoamide (steps 2 to 4), CoA (step 3), FAD and NAD⁺ (step 4).
cards.why: Mnemonic: Tender Loving Care For Nancy.
cards.quote: Count the coenzymes you just used: TPP (step 1), lipoamide (steps 2 to 4), CoA (step 3), FAD and NAD⁺ (step 4).
cards.section: Following one pyruvate: two tracks on one arm

cards.front: Which vitamin supplies each of PDC's coenzymes TPP, CoA, FAD and NAD⁺?
cards.back: TPP: thiamine B1. CoA: pantothenate B5. FAD: riboflavin B2. NAD⁺: niacin B3. Lipoic acid is made by the body, so it is not a true vitamin.
cards.quote: Four come from vitamins you must eat: thiamine B1 (TPP, at E1), pantothenate B5 (CoA, at E2), riboflavin B2 (FAD, at E3) and niacin B3 (NAD⁺, at E3).
cards.section: Following one pyruvate: two tracks on one arm

cards.front: No PDC step uses molecular O₂. A cell is deprived of oxygen. Predict what happens to PDC flux, and why.
cards.back: PDC stops. Without O₂ the electron transport chain cannot turn NADH back into NAD⁺, so step 4 at E3 runs out of acceptor and the relay stalls.
cards.quote: PDC needs oxygen only indirectly: the electron transport chain must turn NADH back into NAD⁺, or step 4 runs out of acceptor and the relay stops.
cards.section: Following one pyruvate: two tracks on one arm

cards.front: What is substrate channeling in PDC, and why is it better than three free enzymes?
cards.back: E1 and E3 dock on the E2 core within reach of the swinging arm, so intermediates pass from site to site without diffusing into solution, where they could drift away or be lost to side reactions.
cards.quote: So the intermediates never diffuse into solution, where they could drift away or be lost to side reactions.
cards.section: One machine, so nothing floats free

cards.front: Describe the E2 core of eukaryotic PDC, and the E. coli version.
cards.back: Eukaryotes: 60 subunits arranged as a pentagonal dodecahedron (in mammals some positions are E3BP). E. coli: a 24-subunit cube. Eukaryotic PDC is roughly 10 megadaltons.
cards.quote: E2 forms a core of 60 subunits arranged as a pentagonal dodecahedron
cards.section: Size and docking of the complex

cards.front: Design: compare acetyl-CoA output from intact PDC with an equal amount of E1, E2 and E3 freed from the complex. Predict the result and the principle it tests.
cards.back: The intact complex should make acetyl-CoA more efficiently. Free enzymes are no longer within reach of the lipoamide arm, so intermediates cannot be handed directly from site to site.
cards.why: Rests on substrate channeling: docking on the E2 core keeps every active site within the arm's reach.
cards.quote: E2 forms the core, and E1 and E3 dock onto it, close enough for the arm to reach every active site.
cards.section: One machine, so nothing floats free

cards.front: Why must gluconeogenesis bypass PDC instead of running it backward, and where does it start?
cards.back: In animals the reaction is irreversible: no enzyme runs it backward, so acetyl-CoA cannot become pyruvate. Gluconeogenesis must start on the near side, e.g. from pyruvate (or other entry points), with pyruvate carboxylase and PEPCK carrying it back to PEP.
cards.quote: In animals this reaction is irreversible: no enzyme runs it backward, and acetyl-CoA cannot become pyruvate again.

cards.front: PDC energy ledger (ΔG°′, pH 7): the oxidation gives about −50 kJ/mol, storing the acetyl as a thioester costs about +31, and the overall reaction is about −33. What does losing CO₂ contribute?
cards.back: Setup: −33 = −50 + 31 + x, so x = −33 + 19 = about −14 kJ/mol. Found by difference, so approximate.
cards.quote: Building the thioester spends most of the oxidation's drop, about 31 of the 50.

cards.front: If PDC released free acetate instead of storing it as a thioester on CoA, what would the overall ΔG°′ be, using the ledger (oxidation about −50, thioester about +31, CO₂ loss about −14 kJ/mol)?
cards.back: Drop the +31 thioester cost: −50 + (−14) = about −64 kJ/mol, instead of about −33.
cards.why: The thioester spends most of the oxidation's drop to wind the acetyl-CoA spring.
cards.quote: Storing the acetyl group as a thioester, instead of letting it go as free acetate

cards.front: PDC's overall ΔG°′ is about −33 kJ/mol. Estimate its equilibrium constant at body temperature (310 K, R = 8.314 J/mol·K).
cards.back: K = e^(−ΔG°′/RT) = e^(33,000 / (8.314 × 310)) = e^12.8, about 4 × 10⁵. The reaction runs only forward in practice.
cards.quote: so far toward the products that in practice the reaction runs only forward.

cards.front: The acetate/acetaldehyde couple has E°′ = −0.581 V and NAD⁺/NADH has E°′ = −0.320 V. Calculate ΔG°′ for moving two electrons from the aldehyde to NAD⁺ (F = 96.485 kJ/mol·V).
cards.quote: The −50 kJ/mol comes from the reduction potentials of the acetate/acetaldehyde couple (−0.581 V) and NAD⁺ (−0.320 V).

cards.front: Hydrolysis of acetyl-CoA has a ΔG°′ of about {{c1::−31 kJ/mol}}, roughly that of ATP (−30.5); an ordinary oxygen ester gives only about −21.
cards.quote: The +31 line is the same number you get back when you hydrolyze acetyl-CoA: about −31 kJ/mol, roughly ATP's −30.5.

cards.front: Why does hydrolyzing a thioester like acetyl-CoA release more energy than hydrolyzing an oxygen ester?
cards.back: The thioester gets little resonance stabilization, so its hydrolysis products are much more stable than it is. An oxygen ester is stabilized by its lone pairs, so less is released.
cards.why: Sulfur is larger than oxygen, so its orbitals overlap the carbonyl carbon poorly.
cards.quote: sulfur is larger than oxygen, so its orbitals overlap the carbonyl carbon poorly, whereas an oxygen ester's lone pairs stabilize its C=O.

cards.front: Is the energy of acetyl-CoA stored in its thioester bond?
cards.back: No. Breaking a bond always costs energy. Hydrolysis releases energy because the products, acetate and CoA-SH, are much more stable than the poorly stabilized thioester.
cards.quote: This is not energy stored in the bond; breaking a bond always costs energy.

cards.front: A fasting person oxidizes even-chain fatty acids to acetyl-CoA. Can that acetyl-CoA supply net glucose? Which parts of a fat can?
cards.back: No net glucose: acetyl-CoA is past the irreversible PDC gate and can never become pyruvate. The exceptions are glycerol and the propionyl-CoA from the end of odd-chain fatty-acid breakdown.
cards.quote: Two parts of a fat are the exceptions: its glycerol, and the propionyl-CoA made at the end of odd-chain fatty-acid breakdown.

cards.front: Plants and bacteria can make glucose from acetyl-CoA, but animals cannot. What route do they have?
cards.back: The glyoxylate cycle, which makes new oxaloacetate (and so glucose) from acetyl-CoA. Animals lack it.
cards.quote: animals lack the glyoxylate cycle, the separate route plants and bacteria use to make new oxaloacetate (and so glucose) from acetyl-CoA.

cards.front: Mitochondrial NADH/NAD⁺ rises sharply while acetyl-CoA stays normal. Which PDC enzyme is directly slowed by product inhibition, and which track backs up?
cards.back: E3, because NADH competes with NAD⁺ there. The electron track backs up, and the relay slows. (The parallel brake is acetyl-CoA competing with CoA at E2, on the carbon track.)
cards.quote: NADH competes with NAD⁺ at E3, backing up the electron track.

cards.front: PDK (pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase) phosphorylates a serine on E1 and switches the complex {{c1::OFF}}; the phosphatase PDP switches it back on.
cards.quote: A dedicated kinase, PDK (pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase), phosphorylates a serine on E1 and switches the complex OFF.

cards.front: How does PDK sense the cell's ATP/ADP ratio?
cards.back: ATP is PDK's substrate and ADP competes with it, so a high ATP/ADP ratio speeds PDK and a high ADP slows it.
cards.quote: ATP is its substrate and ADP competes with it, so PDK reads the ATP/ADP ratio.

cards.front: A well-fed liver mitochondrion has a high ATP/ADP ratio, high NADH and high acetyl-CoA. Predict E1's phosphorylation state and whether the PDC gate is open.
cards.back: E1 is phosphorylated and the gate is closed. These plenty signals stimulate PDK, and at PDC phosphorylation inactivates. They also reinforce the product brake.
cards.quote: Note the direction: here phosphorylation inactivates, the same convention as glycogen synthase.

cards.front: Pyruvate and ADP accumulate in the mitochondrial matrix. Predict the effect on PDK, PDP and PDC activity.
cards.back: Pyruvate and ADP inhibit PDK, so PDP wins: E1 is dephosphorylated and the gate opens, letting the pyruvate through to acetyl-CoA.
cards.quote: the kinase is stimulated by a high ATP/ADP ratio and by high acetyl-CoA and NADH, and inhibited by pyruvate and ADP.

cards.front: A skeletal muscle starts contracting hard. Predict what its cytosolic Ca²⁺ rise does to PDC, and by what route.
cards.back: PDC turns on. Some Ca²⁺ enters the matrix and activates the phosphatase PDP1, which dephosphorylates E1, so acetyl-CoA surges into the citric acid cycle when ATP is needed.
cards.quote: A contracting muscle fills with Ca²⁺; some is taken up into the mitochondrial matrix, where it switches on the phosphatase (the PDP1 isoform).

cards.front: Why do pyruvate and lactate accumulate in beriberi, and which other enzymes fail?
cards.back: No thiamine means no TPP, so E1 cannot decarboxylate pyruvate and the carbon track stops before it starts. TPP-dependent α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase fail too.
cards.quote: Pyruvate and lactate pile up, and the nervous and cardiovascular systems suffer.

cards.front: A severely malnourished, alcohol-dependent patient with normal blood sugar needs IV glucose. Predict the risk of giving glucose alone, and the fix.
cards.back: Without TPP, E1 cannot process the extra pyruvate, so the sugar load can worsen lactic acidosis and has been reported to precipitate Wernicke's. Give thiamine before or with the glucose.
cards.why: Glucose for dangerously low blood sugar is not delayed to wait for thiamine.
cards.quote: This is why a malnourished or alcohol-dependent patient should get thiamine before or with a glucose drip

cards.front: Arsenite bridges the two –SH groups of reduced lipoamide, the state the arm is in after PDC step 3. Which track stops first, and why does the other stop too?
cards.back: The electron track stops: the locked arm cannot pass its electrons to E3, so no NADH forms and the S–S is never restored. The carbon track then stops, because an unreset arm cannot accept the next acetyl group.
cards.quote: Then the carbon track stops too, because an arm that cannot be reset cannot accept the next acetyl group.

cards.front: Compare thiamine deficiency and arsenite poisoning at PDC: which enzyme step and which track does each block first?
cards.back: Thiamine deficiency blocks E1 (no TPP), stopping the carbon track before it starts. Arsenite locks reduced lipoamide, stopping the electron track at the E3 hand-off, then the carbon track. Both end with the relay stalled.
cards.why: Rule: each failure breaks one of the two tracks, and a stall anywhere stops the relay.
cards.quote: Each failure below breaks one of the two tracks, and a stall anywhere stops the relay.

cards.front: An individual has a genetic E3 (dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase) deficiency. Predict the blood findings, and explain why more than PDC is affected.
cards.back: Lactic acidosis, often with raised branched-chain amino acids and α-ketoglutarate. PDC, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and the branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase share one E3, so the electron track stops in all three.
cards.quote: Patients show lactic acidosis, often with raised branched-chain amino acids and α-ketoglutarate.

cards.front: In a tumor where HIF-1α drives up PDK and pyruvate is shunted to lactate despite ample oxygen, a drug blocks PDK. Predict the change in E1, acetyl-CoA formation and lactate output.
cards.back: E1 should be dephosphorylated by PDP and turn on, so more pyruvate becomes acetyl-CoA and less is shunted to lactate in many such tumors.
cards.why: Rests on PDK phosphorylation inactivating E1. Some tumors already keep substantial PDC activity, so the effect would vary.
cards.quote: in many tumors HIF-1α (a low-oxygen transcription factor that many tumors keep switched on) drives up PDK, E1 is held largely phosphorylated and off

cards.front: α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase runs the same E1 → arm → E2 → E3 relay as PDC. Predict whether it is affected by (a) arsenite, (b) E3 deficiency, (c) high PDK activity.
cards.back: (a) Likely yes: it runs the same arm relay and uses the same lipoamide arm. (b) Yes: it shares the same E3. (c) No: it is not controlled by phosphorylation.
cards.quote: The phosphorylation switch is not shared: α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase is not controlled by phosphorylation.
